lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Gaseous exchange is getting oxygen from air and removing carbon dioxide.
  • In leaves most exchange occurs through stomata; in humans it occurs in alveoli.
  • The trachea divides into two bronchi; alveoli are surrounded by capillaries.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration in blood is the primary stimulus for breathing.
  • Emphysema breaks down alveolar walls and reduces exchange surface.

Q: The process of gaseous exchange involves:

(a) Breakdown of C-H bonds to yield energy (b) Physical movements that take air in and out of body (c) Getting oxygen from the air and removing carbon dioxide (d) Transport of oxygen by the blood to different parts of the body
Correct answer: Getting oxygen from the air and removing carbon dioxide

Q: Most of the gaseous exchange in a leaf occurs through:

(a) Stomata (b) General surface (c) Cuticle (d) Lenticels
Correct answer: Stomata

Q: How many bronchi are there in the air passageway?

(a) One (b) Two (c) Many (d) None
Correct answer: Two

Q: Where does the gaseous exchange occur in humans?

(a) Pharynx (b) Trachea (c) Bronchi (d) Alveoli
Correct answer: Alveoli

Q: Which structure actively helps in taking the air out of lungs?

(a) Nasal cavity (b) Bronchus (c) Bronchiole (d) Diaphragm
Correct answer: Diaphragm

Q: The primary chemical stimulus for breathing is the concentration of:

(a) Carbon dioxide in blood (b) Oxygen in blood (c) Carbon dioxide in muscles (d) Oxygen in muscles
Correct answer: Carbon dioxide in blood

Q: Point out the FALSE statement about respiration.

(a) Gases can easily pass through the walls of the alveoli (b) Gas exchange in lungs is very efficient because lungs provide large surface area (c) In emphysema the walls of alveoli break and there is more surface area (d) Dust particles can damage the lung by irritating the inner alveoli surface
Correct answer: In emphysema the walls of alveoli break and there is more surface area

Q: A disease involving the breakdown of air sacs of the lungs is:

(a) Pneumonia (b) Bronchitis (c) Asthma (d) Emphysema
Correct answer: Emphysema

Q: Which process does NOT occur in the nasal cavity?

(a) Trapping of large dust particles (b) Humidification of the inhaled air (c) Warming of the inhaled air (d) Exchange of gases
Correct answer: Exchange of gases

Q: What type of blood vessels surrounds the alveoli?

(a) Artery (b) Arteriole (c) Capillary (d) Vein
Correct answer: Capillary

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Breathing is physical and releases no energy; cellular respiration is biochemical and releases ATP.
  • Air path: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, two bronchi, bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli.
  • A stoma is a leaf pore with two guard cells; a lenticel is a bark pore without guard cells that stays open.

Q: 1. Differentiate between breathing and cellular respiration.

Breathing is a physical process in which air is taken in and given out of the body; it involves no chemical change and releases no energy. Cellular respiration is a biochemical process inside cells in which C-H bonds of food are broken by oxidation-reduction reactions and energy is released as ATP, producing carbon dioxide and water.

Q: 2. Trace the path of air from the nasal cavity to the alveoli.

Air enters through the nostrils into the nasal cavity, passes into the pharynx, then through the larynx into the trachea. The trachea divides into two bronchi, each entering a lung and branching into bronchioles. The bronchioles end in alveolar ducts which open into clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli, where gaseous exchange takes place.

Q: 3. How will you differentiate between a stoma and a lenticel?

A stoma is a tiny pore in the epidermis of leaves and young stems, bordered by two guard cells which regulate its opening; most gaseous exchange in leaves occurs through stomata. A lenticel is a raised pore in the bark of woody stems and roots, formed of loosely arranged cells without guard cells; it remains open and allows exchange of gases in older woody parts.

A biochemical process inside cells that releases ATP
A process that breaks C-H bonds by oxidation
A process involving chemical change in food
mcqs.why: Breathing is a physical process of taking air in and out; it involves no chemical change and releases no energy.

mcqs.q: What is cellular respiration?
options: A physical process of moving air in and out of the body
A biochemical process inside cells in which C-H bonds of food are broken and energy is released as ATP
The opening and closing of stomata by guard cells
The movement of air through the trachea only
mcqs.why: Cellular respiration breaks C-H bonds by oxidation-reduction, releasing energy as ATP and producing carbon dioxide and water.

mcqs.q: Which process releases energy as ATP?
mcqs.why: Only cellular respiration releases energy as ATP; breathing is purely physical and releases no energy.

mcqs.why: The path is nasal cavity, then pharynx, then larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and finally alveoli.

mcqs.why: The trachea divides into two bronchi, each entering a lung and branching into bronchioles inside it.

mcqs.why: Bronchioles end in alveolar ducts which open into clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

mcqs.why: Gaseous exchange takes place in the alveoli, where bronchioles end via alveolar ducts.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Leaves use stomata, woody stems and roots use lenticels, roots also absorb soil oxygen.
  • Inhalation: diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume rises, air enters; exhalation reverses this.
  • Bronchitis inflames bronchi; emphysema breaks alveolar walls; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid.
  • Tobacco tar paralyses cilia and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carriage by blood.

Q: 1. How do the different parts of the plant body exchange gases with the environment?

Leaves and young stems exchange gases through stomata in their epidermis, and the inner mesophyll cells also have air spaces among them for gas movement. Woody stems and roots exchange gases through lenticels in the bark. Roots also take up oxygen dissolved in soil air through their general surface and root hairs. In this way every living cell of the plant gets oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide.

Q: 2. Write down the steps of inhalation and exhalation.

Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs upward and outward, the volume of the chest cavity increases, pressure inside the lungs falls, and air rushes in. Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, the ribs move downward and inward, the chest volume decreases, pressure in the lungs rises, and air is pushed out.

Q: 3. State the signs and symptoms, causes and treatments of bronchitis, emphysema and pneumonia.

Bronchitis is the inflammation of the bronchi, caused mainly by viral or bacterial infection and by smoke; its symptoms are cough, mucus production and chest discomfort, and it is treated with rest, fluids and antibiotics when bacterial. Emphysema is caused mainly by long smoking; the walls of alveoli break down, causing breathlessness, and there is no cure except stopping smoking and using bronchodilators and oxygen. Pneumonia is the infection of the lungs, usually by the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae; it causes fever, cough and difficulty in breathing as alveoli fill with fluid, and it is treated with antibiotics and supportive care.

Q: 4. How does the tobacco smoke damage the respiratory system?

Tobacco smoke contains tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide. Tar coats and irritates the lining of the air passages and alveoli, paralyses the cilia so mucus and dust accumulate, and promotes chronic bronchitis and lung cancer. Smoke destroys the walls of alveoli causing emphysema, while carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. Continuous smoking therefore progressively destroys the respiratory surface and lung function.

mcqs.why: Leaves and young stems exchange gases through stomata in their epidermis, with air spaces among mesophyll cells.

lessons.title: The Terms to Know
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alveolus is the microscopic air sac where gas exchange between air and blood occurs.
  • Diaphragm is the dome-shaped main muscle of breathing below the lungs.
  • Trachea is the windpipe kept open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
  • Emphysema breaks down alveolar walls; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid.

Q: Define: Alveolar duct

The tiny tube at the end of a bronchiole which opens into a cluster of alveoli.

Q: Define: Alveolus

A microscopic air sac at the end of the bronchioles where exchange of gases between air and blood takes place.

Q: Define: Asthma

A respiratory disorder in which the bronchioles constrict and produce excess mucus, causing difficulty in breathing.

Q: Define: Breathing

The physical process of taking air in (inhalation) and giving air out (exhalation) of the lungs.

Q: Define: Bronchioles

The fine branches of bronchi inside the lungs which end in alveolar ducts.

Q: Define: Bronchitis

The inflammation of the bronchi, usually due to infection or smoke, marked by cough and mucus.

Q: Define: Bronchus

One of the two tubes into which the trachea divides, each carrying air into a lung.

Q: Define: Diaphragm

The dome-shaped muscular sheet below the lungs which is the main muscle of breathing.

Q: Define: Emphysema

A lung disease in which the walls of alveoli break down, reducing the surface for gaseous exchange.

Q: Define: Exhalation

The process of breathing air out of the lungs when the chest cavity decreases in volume.

Q: Define: Gaseous exchange

The taking in of oxygen and giving out of carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment.

Q: Define: Inhalation

The process of taking air into the lungs when the chest cavity increases in volume.

Q: Define: Larynx

The voice box; the short passage at the top of the trachea, between the pharynx and the trachea, which contains the vocal cords and through which air passes from the pharynx into the trachea.

Q: Define: Lenticels

Raised pores in the bark of woody stems and roots through which gases are exchanged.

Q: Define: Nasal cavity

The space inside the nose where air is filtered, warmed and moistened.

Q: Define: Nostril

The external opening of the nasal cavity through which air enters and leaves.

Q: Define: Pneumonia

An infection of the lungs in which the alveoli become inflamed and fill with fluid.

Q: Define: Trachea

The windpipe; the tube carrying air from the larynx to the bronchi, kept open by C-shaped cartilage rings.

Q: Define: Vocal cords

Two folds of tissue in the larynx which vibrate to produce sound.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Bright light: indicator turns purple as photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide; darkness: yellow as respiration releases it.
  • Breathing rate rises after exercise because muscles produce more carbon dioxide.
  • Vital capacity is about 3.5 to 4.5 litres in a healthy young adult.
  • Exhaled air turns limewater milky faster, showing it has far more carbon dioxide.

Q: Activity 1. Investigate the effect of light on the net gaseous exchange from leaf, by using bicarbonate as the indicator.

Place a leafy shoot in a tube containing hydrogencarbonate indicator solution and keep identical tubes in bright light, dim light and darkness. In bright light photosynthesis exceeds respiration, carbon dioxide is absorbed and the indicator turns purple; in darkness only respiration occurs, carbon dioxide is released and the indicator turns yellow. This shows that light changes the net direction of gaseous exchange in a leaf.

Q: Activity 2. Investigate the breathing rate at rest and after exercise.

Count the number of breaths per minute of a volunteer sitting at rest, then after two minutes of running or skipping count again immediately. The breathing rate after exercise is much higher because the muscles respire faster, produce more carbon dioxide, and the body increases breathing to supply more oxygen and remove the extra carbon dioxide.

Q: Activity 3. Find out how much air a person can take into his lungs.

Fill a large inverted bottle or spirometer jar with water over a trough, and ask the volunteer to take a deep breath and blow all the air out through a tube into the jar in one breath. The volume of water displaced equals the vital capacity of the lungs, which for a healthy young adult is about 3.5 to 4.5 litres.

Q: Activity 4. Demonstrate through experiment that carbon dioxide is exhaled during respiration.

Take two test tubes of clear limewater. Pass fresh air through one with a syringe and ask a volunteer to blow exhaled air through the other with a straw. The limewater receiving exhaled air turns milky much faster, proving that exhaled air contains far more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.

Purple, because carbon dioxide is released

mcqs.why: In bright light photosynthesis exceeds respiration, carbon dioxide is absorbed and the indicator turns purple.

mcqs.why: After exercise muscles have respired faster, producing more carbon dioxide, so breathing increases to supply oxygen.

mcqs.why: Blowing all air into the jar displaces water equal to vital capacity, about 3.5 to 4.5 litres in a young adult.

mcqs.why: The source gives vital capacity of a healthy young adult as about 3.5 to 4.5 litres.

mcqs.why: The faster milky change proves exhaled air contains far more carbon dioxide than inhaled (fresh) air.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Tilling aerates soil so roots get oxygen; waterlogged soil suffocates roots.
  • A ventilator forces air into the lungs at controlled pressure, volume and rate.
  • Exhaust carbon monoxide reduces oxygen transport; particles damage alveoli.
  • Cross ventilation replaces stale air with fresh air and cools rooms naturally.

Q: 1. Evaluate the effects of tilling on roots for better exchange of gases with the soil air.

Tilling loosens the soil and increases the air spaces between its particles, so more oxygen reaches the roots for respiration and carbon dioxide escapes easily. Well-aerated soil therefore supports healthy root growth and better absorption of water and minerals, while compact or waterlogged soil suffocates roots.

Q: 2. Outline the concept of Artificial Ventilator for artificial breathing in patients.

An artificial ventilator is a machine that forces air or oxygen into the lungs of a patient who cannot breathe adequately on his own. It delivers air at controlled pressure, volume and rate through a tube placed in the trachea, and allows exhalation passively, thus maintaining gaseous exchange until natural breathing recovers.

Q: 3. Interpret the dangers of breathing in exhausts of fossil fuels (Petrol and others).

Vehicle and factory exhausts contain carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides and fine particles. Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport, particles irritate and damage the alveoli, and the pollutants aggravate asthma, bronchitis and lung cancer. Chronic exposure therefore seriously damages the respiratory and circulatory systems.

Q: 4. Rationalize the importance of cross ventilation in homes.

Cross ventilation, with openings on opposite sides of a room, keeps fresh air flowing through the house. It removes stale air rich in carbon dioxide, moisture, smoke and germs, and replaces it with oxygen-rich air, reducing respiratory infections and discomfort. It also cools rooms naturally without energy use.

Q: 5. Assess the adverse effects associated with smoking on health.

Smoking causes chronic bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer, damages cilia and alveoli, and its carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen supply to tissues. Nicotine raises blood pressure and heart rate and is addictive. Smoking also harms passive smokers around the smoker and increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.

Q: 6. Point out bad social aspects of smoking.

Smoking exposes family members and the public to harmful passive smoke, creates an unhealthy example for children, wastes household income needed for food and education, causes litter and fire hazards, and its smell and smoke disturb others in public places. It also burdens the health system with preventable diseases.

Q: 1. What are the major organs involved in homeostasis in human body? State the roles of each of these organs.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Proximal tubule reabsorbs all glucose and amino acids, most salts and about 80% of water.
  • Urine formation: pressure filtration, selective re-absorption, tubular secretion.
  • Each kidney has about one million nephrons.
  • ADH increases water reabsorption when blood is concentrated - this is osmoregulation.

Q: 1. Describe the process of selective re-absorption in the kidneys.

After filtration, the filtrate passes through the tubule of the nephron, and useful substances are taken back into the blood capillaries around it. In the proximal tubule all glucose and amino acids, most salts and about 80 percent of water are reabsorbed. In the loop of Henle more water and salts are absorbed, and in the distal tubule and collecting duct further controlled amounts of water and ions are reabsorbed under hormonal control. Only the waste and excess materials remain in the tubule and form urine.

Q: 2. How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?

Plants remove extra water by transpiration through stomata and by guttation through hydathodes at leaf margins. Excess salts and other waste products are stored in bark, old leaves and fruits which are then shed, or are deposited in the heartwood and in cell vacuoles. Some wastes are also excreted through roots into the soil.

Q: 3. What is the functional unit of the kidney? Describe its structure and draw labelled diagram.

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron; each kidney contains about one million nephrons. A nephron consists of a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a knot of capillaries called the glomerulus, followed by a long tubule: the proximal convoluted tubule, the U-shaped loop of Henle, and the distal convoluted tubule, which joins a collecting duct. A labelled diagram should show: Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct and the capillary network around the tubule. (Draw the diagram as shown in Fig. 11 of the book.)

Q: 4. What steps are involved in the formation of urine in the kidneys?

Urine formation occurs in three steps. (1) Pressure filtration: blood pressure forces water, salts, glucose, amino acids and urea from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule, while cells and proteins stay in blood. (2) Selective re-absorption: useful substances and most water are reabsorbed from the tubule into the blood. (3) Tubular secretion: extra wastes such as hydrogen ions, potassium ions and drugs are secreted from blood into the distal tubule. The remaining fluid is urine, which flows to the pelvis of the kidney and then to the bladder.

Q: 5. "Along with excretion, kidneys also play role in Osmoregulation." Comment on this statement.

The statement is correct. Besides removing urea and other wastes, the kidneys precisely control the amount of water and salts in the blood. When blood becomes concentrated, the pituitary releases more ADH, the kidney tubules reabsorb more water and concentrated urine is produced; when blood is dilute, less ADH is released and excess water is excreted. In this way the kidneys keep the osmotic pressure and volume of body fluids constant, which is osmoregulation.

Key Points

  • In dehydration, ADH rises and kidneys produce small, concentrated urine.
  • Stones: lithotripsy or surgery; infections: antibiotics; failure: dialysis or transplant.

Q: 1. Realize the importance of drinking plentiful water daily.

Water is needed for making urine to remove urea and other wastes, for keeping blood volume and concentration normal, for sweating and temperature control, and for all cell activities. Drinking plentiful water daily prevents dehydration, kidney stones and urinary infections, and helps the kidneys work efficiently.

Q: 2. Predict how the kidney helps to overcome the problem of dehydration.

In dehydration the blood becomes concentrated, the pituitary gland releases more ADH, and the kidney tubules reabsorb more water, producing a small volume of concentrated urine. The kidneys also conserve salts, so body water is preserved until drinking restores the balance.

Q: 3. Recognize the right treatments of kidney problems.

Kidney stones are treated by lithotripsy (breaking stones with shock waves) or surgery; kidney infections are treated with antibiotics; and kidney failure is treated by dialysis (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) to remove wastes artificially, and finally by kidney transplantation with a matched donor kidney.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Two coordinations: nervous (fast, targeted) and chemical (slower, longer-lasting, via blood).
  • Components: receptors, coordinators, effectors; messengers are neurons and hormones.
  • Reflex arc: receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, effector.
  • Vitamin A forms rhodopsin; its deficiency causes night blindness.

Q: 1. Identify the two types of coordination in living organisms.

The two types of coordination are nervous coordination, carried out by the nervous system through electrical nerve impulses, and chemical coordination, carried out by hormones secreted by endocrine glands and carried by the blood.

Q: 2. Differentiate between the modes of nervous and chemical coordinations.

Nervous coordination is fast, short-lived and precisely targeted: impulses travel along specific neurons to specific effectors. Chemical coordination is slower but longer-lasting and more general: hormones are released into the blood and reach all parts of the body, acting only on target organs having specific receptors.

Q: 3. What are the main components of coordination?

The main components of coordination are: receptors, which detect stimuli; coordinators (brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands), which process information and decide the response; and effectors (muscles and glands), which carry out the response. Neurons and hormones act as the messengers between these components.

Q: 4. Define reflex action and reflex arc.

A reflex action is an immediate, involuntary response to a stimulus, e.g. pulling the hand away from a hot object. The reflex arc is the pathway of the impulse in a reflex: receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron and effector.

Q: 5. Trace the path of a nerve impulse in case of a reflex action.

A stimulus is detected by a receptor, which generates an impulse in a sensory neuron. The impulse enters the spinal cord and passes through an interneuron to a motor neuron. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector (muscle or gland), which responds immediately, e.g. the muscle contracts and the hand is withdrawn.

Q: 6. Describe the pupil reflex in dim and bright light.

In dim light the radial muscles of the iris contract and the circular muscles relax, so the pupil dilates and more light enters the eye. In bright light the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil constricts and less light enters, protecting the retina from damage.

Q: 7. How would you associate the role of vitamin A with vision and effects of its deficiency on retina?

Vitamin A is needed to form rhodopsin, the visual pigment of the rod cells of the retina, which enables vision in dim light. Deficiency of vitamin A reduces rhodopsin formation, causing night blindness; prolonged deficiency also dries the cornea and retina (xerophthalmia) and can lead to complete blindness.

Q: 8. Define the terms; hormone and endocrine system.

A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which acts on a specific target organ to regulate its activity. The endocrine system is the set of all ductless (endocrine) glands of the body, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas and adrenals, which together coordinate body functions chemically.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cerebrum: voluntary actions, memory, senses; cerebellum: balance; medulla: heartbeat and breathing.
  • Neuron: cell body, dendrites (towards body) and axon (away), often with a myelin sheath.
  • Myopia is corrected by concave lenses; hypermetropia by convex lenses.
  • Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it - negative feedback.

Q: 1. Explain what can happen if there is no coordination in the activities of organisms.

Without coordination the different organs would work independently and at cross purposes: muscles would contract without order, glands would secrete without control, and the internal environment would become unstable. The organism would fail to respond to stimuli such as danger, food or temperature change, homeostasis would collapse, and survival would become impossible.

Q: 2. Explain the location and function of these parts of brain; cerebrum, cerebellum, pituitary gland, thalamus, hypothalamus, medulla oblongata.

Cerebrum: the largest, upper part of the forebrain; it controls voluntary actions, memory, intelligence and senses. Cerebellum: below the cerebrum at the back; it coordinates muscle movements and maintains body balance and posture. Pituitary gland: attached below the hypothalamus; the master gland secreting hormones that control other glands, growth and reproduction. Thalamus: in the forebrain; it relays sensory impulses to the cerebrum. Hypothalamus: below the thalamus; it controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and the pituitary gland. Medulla oblongata: the lowest part of the brain connecting to the spinal cord; it controls involuntary actions like heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure.

Q: 3. Define neuron and describe the structure of a general neuron.

A neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system which conducts nerve impulses. It has three parts: the cell body, containing the nucleus and cytoplasm; dendrites, short branched processes which carry impulses towards the cell body; and the axon, a long fibre which carries impulses away from the cell body to other neurons or effectors. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier, which speed up conduction.

Q: 4. Describe the structure of human eye.

The eye is a spherical ball with three layers: the outer sclera, whose transparent front part is the cornea; the middle choroid, rich in blood vessels, whose front part forms the iris with the pupil in its centre, and behind the pupil lies the lens held by ciliary muscles; and the inner retina, containing photoreceptor cells, rods and cones. The space in front of the lens contains aqueous humour and behind it vitreous humour. Light entering through the cornea and pupil is focused by the lens onto the retina, and the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain.

Q: 5. How would you describe the structure of the external, middle and inner ear of man?

The external ear consists of the pinna and the auditory canal ending at the eardrum (tympanum). The middle ear is an air-filled cavity containing three small bones (ossicles): malleus, incus and stapes, and it is connected to the throat by the Eustachian tube. The inner ear consists of the coiled cochlea, concerned with hearing, and the semicircular canals, concerned with balance; it is filled with fluid and contains sensory hair cells.

Q: 6. What are short sight and long sight problems and how can these be treated?

Short sight (myopia) is the inability to see distant objects clearly because the image is focused in front of the retina; it is corrected by concave (diverging) lenses. Long sight (hypermetropia) is the inability to see near objects clearly because the image is focused behind the retina; it is corrected by convex (converging) lenses.

Q: 7. Explain the role of ear in the maintenance of balance.

The semicircular canals of the inner ear contain fluid and sensory hair cells. When the head moves, the fluid moves and bends the hair cells, which send impulses to the brain about the direction and speed of movement. The brain then orders the muscles to adjust posture, so body balance is maintained.

Q: 8. Relate the contribution of Ibn-al-Haitham and Al-Ibn-Isa with knowledge about the structure of eye and treatment of various ophthalmic diseases.

Ibn-al-Haitham (Alhazen) explained correctly, in his Book of Optics, that vision occurs when light from objects enters the eye, rejecting the old idea that rays leave the eye; he described the parts of the eye and the process of image formation. Ali ibn Isa (Al-Ibn-Isa) wrote a famous textbook of ophthalmology describing the structure of the eye and the treatment of many eye diseases, including surgical methods, which remained a standard reference for centuries.

Q: 9. Outline the major glands of the endocrine system (pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal, gonads), with name of their hormones and their functions.

Pituitary: growth hormone (body growth) and many tropic hormones controlling other glands. Thyroid: thyroxin (controls metabolic rate) and calcitonin (lowers blood calcium). Pancreas (islets of Langerhans): insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises blood glucose). Adrenals: adrenaline (prepares body for emergency), corticosteroids and aldosterone (salt and water balance). Gonads: testes secrete testosterone (male characters and sperm production); ovaries secrete estrogen and progesterone (female characters and menstrual cycle).

Q: 10. Describe negative feedback with reference to insulin and glucagon.

Negative feedback keeps a quantity near a set point by reversing any change. When blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas secretes insulin, which makes cells take up glucose and the liver store glycogen, so glucose falls and insulin secretion stops. When blood glucose falls, glucagon is secreted, which breaks down glycogen to glucose, raising the level again. The two hormones thus oppose each other and hold blood glucose constant.

Q: 11. Explain how adrenaline may be involved in exercise and emergency conditions.

In emergency or exercise, the adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline, which increases heart rate and blood pressure, diverts blood to the muscles, dilates the air passages so more oxygen enters, and releases glucose from liver glycogen. These changes supply the muscles with extra oxygen and energy for rapid action, the 'fight or flight' response.

Q: 12. Enlist the important symptoms and treatments of paralysis and epilepsy.

Paralysis is the loss of muscle function in part of the body, often due to damage to the brain, spinal cord or nerves (e.g. by stroke or polio); symptoms are inability to move the affected part and loss of sensation, and treatment includes treating the cause, medicines and regular physiotherapy. Epilepsy is a brain disorder marked by repeated seizures or fits due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain; it is treated with anti-epileptic medicines taken regularly, and surgery in some cases.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Plants coordinate only chemically, so responses are slow growth movements.
  • Healthy blood glucose is near 90 mg/100 ml; diabetes keeps it much higher.
  • Reaction time by the ruler test is about 0.2 seconds.
  • Pupil constricts within about a second when a spotlight is flashed.

Q: 1. Analyze why plants (like sunflower) have a very slow response to stimuli.

Plants have no nervous system; their coordination is chemical, through hormones (e.g. auxins) which move slowly by diffusion and bring about slow growth responses such as bending towards light. Because the response depends on growth and hormone transport rather than fast nerve impulses, it takes hours or days instead of fractions of a second.

Q: 2. Visualize nervous and hormonal coordination by comparing electrical transmission in wires with the transmission of nerve impulse in neurons and by comparing convection currents in liquids with the hormonal transmission in blood.

A nerve impulse resembles an electric signal in a wire: it travels rapidly along a fixed path (the neuron, like a wire) to one definite destination and stops quickly. Hormonal coordination resembles convection currents in a liquid: the hormone is poured into the blood and is carried everywhere the blood flows, slowly and generally, affecting all tissues but acting only where specific receptors exist, and its effect lasts longer, like warmth spreading through a heated liquid.

Q: 3. Compare the BGC (blood glucose concentration) of healthy person with a patient suffering from Diabetes mellitus.

In a healthy person blood glucose stays near 90 mg/100 ml: after a meal it rises slightly and insulin quickly brings it back to normal. In a diabetes mellitus patient, due to lack of insulin or its failure, blood glucose remains much higher than normal, rises steeply after meals, and glucose even appears in the urine; without treatment it damages eyes, kidneys and nerves.

Q: Activity 1. Record the difference in quickness of response of the two types of coordination (by asking a student to say a few words in front of the class and observe the change in heartbeat).

When the student suddenly speaks before the class, nervous responses (turning of heads, eye movements) occur within a fraction of a second, while the change in heartbeat, caused by adrenaline released into the blood, takes several seconds to appear and fades slowly. This records that nervous coordination is much quicker and shorter-lived than hormonal coordination.

Q: Activity 2. Perform an experiment in which a scale held at its lower end between the thumb and index finger is allowed to fall and then recording the time taken to catch it again.

One student holds a ruler at its top so that its lower end is between the partner's thumb and finger without touching. The ruler is dropped without warning and the partner catches it; the distance it fell, read from the scale, gives the reaction time (about 0.2 s for most students). Repeating with practice shows slightly faster catching, demonstrating the speed of nervous coordination.

Q: Activity 3. Identify different parts and draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of the eye of sheep or bull.

In the dissected eye the parts identified are: sclera (outer white coat), cornea (transparent front), choroid (dark middle layer), iris and pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, aqueous and vitreous humours. The labelled diagram drawn from it should show the lens focusing light on the retina at the back, with the optic nerve leaving from the blind spot. (Labels as in the book's Fig. of the eye.)

Q: Activity 4. Perform an experiment in which the shin muscle of a frog is made to contract in a Petri dish filled with methylene blue and using 12 V, DC current.

The frog muscle preparation is placed in the dish and brief electric shocks from a 12 V DC source are applied through electrodes. Each shock makes the muscle contract, showing that muscles respond to electrical stimulation like the nerve impulses they normally receive; methylene blue stains the tissue so the muscle and nerve can be seen clearly. (Performed only as a teacher-supervised demonstration where permitted.)

Q: Activity 5. Check the vision of a friend to diagnose whether he/she is suffering from long or short-sightedness.

Ask the friend to read a letter chart from a fixed distance and then a book at normal reading distance. If distant letters are blurred but near reading is clear, the friend is short-sighted (myopic); if near print is difficult but distant objects are clear, the friend is long-sighted (hypermetropic). A confirmed diagnosis and lens prescription, however, require an eye specialist.

Q: Activity 6. Perform an experiment in which one student flashes a spotlight into the eye of another and record the time taken for the eye to contract its pupil.

In dim light the subject's pupil is wide. When the spotlight is flashed into the eye, the pupil constricts almost immediately, within about a second, by the pupil reflex. Recording the time with a stopwatch for several trials shows the reflex is fast and involuntary, protecting the retina from sudden bright light.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cerebrum plans movements and cerebellum fine-tunes them; practice speeds coordination.
  • Light travels at 300,000 km/s, sound at 343 m/s - thunder lags about 3 s per km.
  • Human insulin is now made in bacteria by genetic engineering.
  • Sprint energy largely comes from anaerobic respiration, building lactic acid.

Q: 1. Explain the way nervous system helps to coordinate complex and intricate movements of hand to play a piano, or write alphabets.

Playing the piano or writing needs precise, timed contraction of many small hand muscles. Sensory receptors in the fingers and eyes send continuous feedback to the brain; the cerebrum plans the sequence and the cerebellum fine-tunes the force and timing of each movement through motor neurons. Practice makes these coordinated pathways faster and more accurate.

Q: 2. Analyze the way this knowledge has helped humans to train dogs and domesticated animals to perform specific tasks.

Training uses the animal's nervous coordination and learning: a desired action is repeatedly paired with a signal and a reward, forming conditioned reflexes in the brain. In this way dogs are trained to guide the blind, detect smells for police work, and herd animals, and other domesticated animals learn to perform specific useful tasks.

Q: 3. Explain the reason for salivation of mouth when a favourite food item is imagined.

Salivation at the sight, smell or even thought of favourite food is a conditioned reflex. Past experience has associated these stimuli with eating, so the brain, through autonomic nerves, orders the salivary glands to secrete saliva in advance, preparing the mouth for digestion even before food arrives.

Q: 4. Justify the time difference between seeing the flash of lightening and hearing the roar of a thunderstorm.

Light travels at about 300,000 km/s while sound travels at only about 343 m/s in air. The flash of lightning therefore reaches the eyes almost instantly, whereas the thunder takes roughly 3 seconds to travel each kilometre from the storm. This difference in the speeds of light and sound fully explains why the flash is seen before the thunder is heard.

Q: 5. Explain why and how eyes are important to survival in wild animals.

Eyes give wild animals vision to locate food, detect predators and prey at a distance, judge distances for catching or escaping, and navigate their habitat. Herbivores have eyes on the sides of the head for a wide field of view to spot danger, while predators have forward-facing eyes for binocular vision and accurate attack; survival of both depends on this sense.

Q: 6. Explain how colour blindness could be a hurdle for aircraft pilots.

Pilots must instantly and correctly read coloured signal lights, runway and cockpit indicator colours, navigation lights of other aircraft and colour-coded charts and weather displays. A colour-blind pilot may confuse red and green signals, which can cause fatal errors in take-off, landing and navigation, so airlines require normal colour vision for pilots.

Q: 7. Conceptualize how scientific advancement has helped to solve the problem of diabetes.

Science identified insulin as the missing hormone and first extracted it from animal pancreases for injections. Genetic engineering now produces pure human insulin in bacteria on a large scale, and modern glucometers, insulin pumps, diet planning and new medicines allow patients to monitor and control blood glucose accurately, greatly reducing the complications of diabetes.

Q: 8. Write a paper on the changes in body while performing an exercise like running a 100m sprint race.

During a 100 m sprint the nervous system fires the leg muscles at maximum rate; adrenaline is released, heart rate and breathing rate rise sharply, blood is diverted from the gut to the muscles, and glycogen is broken down rapidly to glucose. Much energy comes from anaerobic respiration, so lactic acid accumulates and body temperature rises with sweating. After the race, heavy breathing continues for some time to repay the oxygen debt and remove lactic acid.

Q: 9. Relate how the knowledge of nervous system has helped humans to treat diseases like epilepsy, paralysis.

Understanding that epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain led to anti-epileptic drugs that stabilize neuron activity, and to brain surgery and stimulation therapies. Knowledge of nerve pathways and regeneration guides the treatment of paralysis through surgery, medicines and physiotherapy, and devices such as nerve stimulators and prosthetics controlled by nerve signals.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cartilage is flexible, has chondrocytes, no blood vessels and no calcium salts; bone is hard with osteocytes and calcium salts.
  • Skeleton supports the body, protects brain, heart and lungs, and its bones act as levers for movement.
  • Osteoporosis is loss of bone mass and density; arthritis is inflammation of joints.
  • Biceps contracts to flex the forearm while triceps relaxes; triceps contracts to extend it.

Q: 1. Differentiate between cartilage and bone.

Cartilage is a flexible, soft connective tissue with cells (chondrocytes) embedded in a matrix of collagen; it has no blood vessels and no calcium salts, and it covers the ends of bones and forms the nose and ear. Bone is a hard, rigid connective tissue whose matrix contains calcium salts; its cells (osteocytes) lie in lacunae, it has a rich blood supply, and it forms the skeleton that supports and protects the body.

Q: 2. What is the role of skeleton in support and movement?

The skeleton forms the framework that supports the body and maintains its shape, and it protects delicate organs such as the brain, heart and lungs. Its bones act as levers and its joints allow movement when the attached muscles contract and relax. In this way the skeleton makes locomotion and all body movements possible.

Q: 3. How would you differentiate between osteoporosis and arthritis?

Osteoporosis is the loss of bone mass and density due to decreased calcium and protein in bones, making them porous and easily breakable; it is common in old age and after menopause. Arthritis is the inflammation of joints, causing pain, stiffness and swelling; its types include osteoarthritis (wearing of cartilage) and rheumatoid arthritis (an autoimmune inflammation).

Q: 4. Label the biceps and triceps in the following diagrams and also mention their contracted or relaxed states.

In the upper diagram the forearm is flexed (bent upward): the biceps (front muscle of the upper arm, upper label) is contracted and shortened, while the triceps (back muscle, lower label) is relaxed. In the lower diagram the forearm is extended (straightened): the biceps is relaxed and the triceps is contracted. Thus biceps is the flexor and triceps is the extensor, and the two work antagonistically.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Axial skeleton has 80 bones: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.
  • Appendicular skeleton has 126 bones: pectoral and pelvic girdles with the limbs.
  • Joints are immovable, slightly movable, or freely movable (hinge and ball-and-socket).
  • Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
  • Biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair because muscles can only pull.

Q: 1. What are the main components of the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton of human?

The axial skeleton (80 bones) consists of the skull (cranial and facial bones), the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum; it protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) consists of the pectoral (shoulder) girdle with the upper limbs and the pelvic girdle with the lower limbs; it is mainly concerned with movement.

Q: 2. Describe the types of joints and give examples.

Joints are of three main types. Immovable (fixed) joints allow no movement, e.g. joints between skull bones. Slightly movable joints allow a little movement, e.g. joints between vertebrae, where cartilage pads separate the bones. Freely movable (synovial) joints allow movement in one or more directions: hinge joints (elbow, knee) move in one plane, while ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow movement in all directions.

Q: 3. What are ligaments and tendons? What function do they perform?

Ligaments are tough, elastic bands of connective tissue that join bone to bone at a joint; they hold the bones in place and prevent dislocation. Tendons are non-elastic cords that attach muscles to bones; they transmit the pull of contracting muscles to the bones so that movement occurs at the joint.

Q: 4. Explain antagonism in muscle action selecting biceps and triceps as example.

Muscles can only pull, not push, so movements are produced by pairs of muscles working oppositely, called antagonistic pairs. When the biceps contracts, the forearm is raised (flexion) and the triceps relaxes. When the triceps contracts, the forearm is lowered (extension) and the biceps relaxes. This opposite working of biceps and triceps is antagonism in muscle action.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Axial skeleton: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; appendicular: girdles and limb bones.
  • Hinge joints move in one plane; ball-and-socket joints move in all directions.
  • Dilute HCl dissolves bone calcium salts leaving collagen; NaOH destroys the protein part.
  • Bone is made of both mineral salts (hardness) and protein (flexibility).

Q: Activity 1. Identify and draw labelled diagrams of different bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton from real specimen models or charts.

From the models/charts identify: axial skeleton — skull (cranium and face), vertebral column, ribs and sternum; appendicular skeleton — pectoral girdle (scapula, clavicle), arm bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges), pelvic girdle and leg bones (femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges). Draw and label each bone in its correct position in the skeleton.

Q: Activity 2. Describe the movement of various human joints through observation of models.

Observing the models: the hinge joints of the elbow and knee bend and straighten in one plane; the ball-and-socket joints of the shoulder and hip rotate and move in all directions; the joints between vertebrae allow only slight bending of the back; and the skull joints do not move at all. Each joint's structure matches the range of movement it allows.

Q: Activity 3. Describe the movement of biceps and triceps through presentation of the movement of your elbow.

Bend your elbow and feel the front muscle of the upper arm (biceps) become hard and short — it is contracted — while the back muscle (triceps) is soft and relaxed. Straighten the arm and the opposite is felt: the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. The elbow thus demonstrates the antagonistic action of biceps and triceps.

Q: Activity 4. Investigate the chemical nature of bone (by putting three pieces of rib bone of lamb or goat in water, NaOH and dilute HCl).

The piece in water stays unchanged (control). The piece in dilute HCl becomes soft and flexible because the acid dissolves the calcium salts, leaving only the protein (collagen) part. The piece in NaOH becomes brittle and weak because the alkali destroys the protein part, leaving mainly the mineral salts. This proves that bone is made of both mineral salts (for hardness) and protein (for flexibility).

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Skeleton supports, protects organs and the nervous system, and acts as levers in daily life.
  • Elbow is a third-class, speed-multiplying lever with the joint as fulcrum.
  • Arthroplasty replaces a damaged hip or knee joint with a metal, ceramic or plastic prosthesis.
  • Prosthetic parts are fixed with cement or bone growth and movement returns with physiotherapy.

Q: 1. Relate your skeleton with its functioning in daily life.

In daily life the skeleton supports the body in standing, sitting and walking, protects the brain, heart and lungs during work and accidents, and its joints and bones act as levers for every movement from writing to lifting loads. The skull and backbone also protect the nervous system which controls all these activities.

Q: 2. Relate the principle of leverage to the action of elbow joint.

The elbow works as a lever: the joint is the fulcrum, the biceps applies the effort close to the joint, and the load (object in the hand) is at the far end. Because the effort arm is short, the biceps must exert a large force, but the hand moves through a large distance and at high speed — a speed-multiplying (third-class) lever.

Q: 3. State the principles of arthroplasty for the replacement of joints.

Arthroplasty is the surgical replacement of a damaged joint (commonly hip or knee) with an artificial joint made of metal, ceramic or plastic. Its principles are: remove the diseased bone and cartilage surfaces, fit prosthetic parts which reproduce the joint's shape and movement, fix them firmly (with cement or bone growth), and restore painless movement through post-operative physiotherapy.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Vegetative propagation uses stem, root or leaves without seeds; other asexual methods use single cells or spores.
  • Cutting and grafting keep the parent's desirable qualities and give faster mature plants.
  • Parthenogenesis: an unfertilized egg develops into a new individual, so it is asexual.
  • Wind-pollinated flowers have light, dry pollen, hanging anthers and large feathery stigmas.
  • National AIDS Control Program was established in 1986-87.

Q: 1. How are the natural and artificial vegetative propagations different from the methods of asexual reproduction in plants?

Natural and artificial vegetative propagation are themselves methods of asexual reproduction in which new plants arise from vegetative parts (stem, root or leaves) without seeds. They differ from the other asexual methods such as binary fission, budding, fragmentation and spore formation, which occur in unicellular organisms, fungi and simple plants through single cells or spores rather than through multicellular vegetative organs of a flowering plant.

Q: 2. Why do gardeners use the methods of cutting and grafting?

Gardeners use cutting and grafting to produce new plants exactly identical to the parent, keeping its desirable qualities such as fruit taste and flower colour. These methods give mature, fruit-bearing plants much faster than seed, allow propagation of seedless or seed-sterile varieties, and grafting combines the strong root system of one plant (stock) with the desirable shoot of another (scion).

Q: 3. "Parthenogenesis is a type of asexual reproduction". Give comments on this statement.

The statement is correct. In parthenogenesis an unfertilized egg develops into a new individual without fusion with a sperm, as in aphids, some bees and some lizards. Since only one parent is involved and no fertilization occurs, it is classed as asexual reproduction, although the structure involved (an egg) is a gamete of the sexual system.

Q: 4. Outline the life cycle of a flowering plant.

The flowering plant (sporophyte) produces flowers in which microspores form pollen grains (male gametophyte) and megaspores form the embryo sac (female gametophyte). Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma; the pollen tube delivers two sperms, and double fertilization produces a zygote and endosperm inside the ovule. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit. The seed germinates to produce the new sporophyte plant, completing the cycle of alternation of generations.

Q: 5. What structural adaptations will you find in a wind-pollinated flower?

Wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull and without nectar or scent; they produce very large quantities of light, dry, smooth pollen. Their anthers are large and hang outside the flower on long filaments, and the stigmas are large, feathery and protruding to catch pollen from the air. Flowers often appear before the leaves, e.g. in grasses and many trees.

Q: 6. Give an introduction of Pakistan's National AIDS Control Program.

The National AIDS Control Program (NACP) was established by the Government of Pakistan in 1986-87 to prevent and control HIV/AIDS in the country. It works through surveillance of high-risk groups, screening of donated blood, awareness campaigns, free testing and counselling centres, and provision of treatment and care to HIV-positive patients, in coordination with provincial AIDS control programs.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Bacteria use binary fission; protozoans use binary/multiple fission; fungi use spores, budding and fragmentation.
  • Natural vegetative propagation uses runners, rhizomes, corms, tubers, bulbs, roots, leaves and suckers.
  • Epigeal germination lifts cotyledons above ground; hypogeal keeps them below ground.
  • Seeds need water, suitable temperature (25-30 C) and oxygen to germinate.
  • Spermatogenesis makes four spermatids from one primary spermatocyte; oogenesis makes one large ovum.

Q: 1. What are the different ways by which prokaryotes, protozoans and fungi reproduce asexually?

Prokaryotes (bacteria) reproduce by binary fission, in which the cell divides into two equal daughter cells, and some form endospores to survive unfavourable conditions. Protozoans reproduce by binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), multiple fission (Plasmodium) and budding in some forms. Fungi reproduce by spore formation (Rhizopus), budding (yeast) and fragmentation of hyphae (many moulds).

Q: 2. Explain the different parts of the plant that help in natural vegetative propagation.

Stems: runners and stolons (grass, strawberry) grow horizontally and root at nodes; rhizomes (ginger) and corms (gladiolus) are underground stems; tubers (potato) bear buds (eyes) which sprout; bulbs (onion, garlic) store food in fleshy leaves around a short stem. Roots: tuberous roots of sweet potato produce buds. Leaves: leaves of Bryophyllum bear buds in their margins which fall and grow into new plants. Suckers (banana, mint) are shoots arising from the base of the stem.

Q: 3. Explain, how the epigeal and hypogeal germinations are different?

In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and carries the cotyledons above the ground, where they become green and photosynthetic, e.g. bean and castor. In hypogeal germination the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain below the ground inside the seed coat, e.g. pea, gram and maize. The difference is thus in which part elongates and whether the cotyledons come out of the soil.

Q: 4. What conditions are necessary for the germination of seeds?

A viable seed needs: adequate water, which softens the seed coat and activates enzymes for digestion of stored food; suitable temperature, usually 25-30 degrees C for most seeds, for enzyme activity; and oxygen (air), for aerobic respiration to release energy. Some seeds additionally need light or a period of cold, and dormancy must first be broken.

Q: 5. Outline the methods of asexual reproduction in animals.

Animals reproduce asexually by: binary fission (Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium), budding (Hydra, sponges), fragmentation and regeneration (Planaria, starfish), and parthenogenesis (aphids, honey bees, in which drones develop from unfertilized eggs). In all these methods only one parent is involved and the offspring are genetically identical to it.

Q: 6. Write a note on the male and female reproductive systems of rabbit.

Male system: a pair of testes in the scrotum produce sperms in seminiferous tubules; sperms pass through the epididymis and vas deferens to the urethra, with secretions added by seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper's glands forming semen, which leaves through the penis. Female system: a pair of ovaries produce eggs in follicles; eggs travel through fallopian tubes (oviducts) where fertilization occurs, then to the two horns of the uterus where embryos develop; the uterus opens through the cervix into the vagina.

Q: 7. Describe the processes of spermatogenesis and oogenesis.

Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of testes: a spermatogonium divides by mitosis, grows into a primary spermatocyte, which undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II to form four spermatids, which mature into sperms; it continues from puberty throughout life. Oogenesis occurs in the ovaries: an oogonium grows into a primary oocyte which begins meiosis before birth; meiosis I completes at ovulation forming a secondary oocyte and a polar body, and meiosis II completes only after fertilization, giving one large ovum; it occurs cyclically from puberty to menopause.

Q: 8. Why do we consider that overpopulation is a global problem?

Overpopulation strains food, water, housing, education and health resources, increases unemployment and poverty, and accelerates deforestation, pollution and loss of biodiversity. When population grows faster than resources and services, the quality of life falls for everyone, which is why it is considered a global problem needing family planning and resource management.

Q: Define: Acrosome

The cap at the head of a sperm containing enzymes to penetrate the egg.

Q: Define: Alternation of generations

The regular alternation of a diploid sporophyte and a haploid gametophyte generation in a plant life cycle.

Q: Define: Androecium

The male part of a flower, made of all its stamens.

Q: Define: Anther

The part of the stamen which produces pollen grains.

Q: Define: Binary fission

Asexual reproduction in which one cell divides into two equal daughter cells.

Q: Define: Budding

Asexual reproduction in which a small outgrowth (bud) from the parent grows and separates as a new individual.

Q: Define: Bulb

A short underground stem surrounded by fleshy storage leaves, e.g. onion.

Q: Define: Calyx

The outermost whorl of a flower, made of sepals.

Q: Define: Carpel

The female reproductive unit of a flower, consisting of stigma, style and ovary.

Q: Define: Cervix

The narrow lower part of the uterus opening into the vagina.

Q: Define: Cloning

Producing genetically identical individuals from a single parent without fertilization.

Q: Define: Corm

A swollen underground stem base storing food, e.g. gladiolus (the book's MCQ applies the term to garlic).

The whorl of petals of a flower, usually coloured to attract pollinators.

A seed leaf which stores food (dicots) or absorbs it (monocots) for the embryo.

A small gland adding fluid to semen in the male reproductive system.

The triploid nucleus formed by fusion of a sperm with the fusion nucleus, which gives rise to endosperm.

The part of the embryo axis above the cotyledons, giving rise to the shoot.

The coiled tube on the testis where sperms are stored and matured.

Germination in which the cotyledons are carried above the ground.

The tube (oviduct) carrying the egg from the ovary towards the uterus; fertilization occurs here.

Q: Define: Follicle

A small sac in the ovary in which an egg develops.

Q: Define: Fragmentation

Asexual reproduction in which the body breaks into pieces, each growing into a new individual.

Q: Define: Fusion nucleus

The diploid nucleus in the embryo sac formed by fusion of two polar nuclei.

Q: Define: Gametogenesis

The formation of gametes (sperms and eggs) by meiosis.

Q: Define: Gametophyte

The haploid, gamete-producing generation in a plant life cycle.

Q: Define: Grafting

Artificial propagation in which a shoot (scion) of one plant is joined to the rooted stem (stock) of another.

Q: Define: Gynoecium

The female part of a flower, made of one or more carpels.

Q: Define: Hilum

The scar on a seed marking its point of attachment to the fruit.

Q: Define: Hypocotyl

The part of the embryo axis below the cotyledons.

Q: Define: Hypogeal germination

Germination in which the cotyledons remain below the ground.

Q: Define: Macrospore

The large spore (megaspore) which develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).

The small pore in the ovule/seed coat through which the pollen tube and water enter.

lessons.title: Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Yeast budding: bud appears, nucleus divides into it, bud enlarges and separates.
  • Onion grows from bulbs, ginger from rhizomes, potato from tubers; maize from seeds.
  • A complete flower has calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
  • Only seeds with water, suitable temperature and air germinate normally.

Q: Activity 1. Identify different stages of budding in the prepared slides of yeast and draw diagrams.

In the yeast slides the stages seen are: a small outgrowth (bud) appears on the parent cell; the nucleus divides and one daughter nucleus enters the bud; the bud enlarges; and finally it separates as a new cell, sometimes forming chains of buds. Draw and label: parent cell, bud, nucleus and chain of cells.

Q: Activity 2. Examine the specimens of onion, corn, ginger and potato and write the mode of their reproduction and describe their cultivation to get new plants.

Onion reproduces by a bulb: the fleshy bulbs are planted in soil and sprout into new plants. Corn (maize) reproduces by seeds: grains are sown in rows in prepared soil. Ginger reproduces by rhizome: pieces of rhizome bearing buds are planted underground. Potato reproduces by stem tuber: tuber pieces with eyes are planted. Except maize, all are vegetative (asexual) methods giving plants identical to the parent.

Q: Activity 3. Identify different parts of flower.

A complete flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx (sepals, usually green), corolla (petals, usually coloured), androecium (stamens: anther and filament, the male part) and gynoecium (carpels: stigma, style and ovary, the female part). Identify and label each part on the dissected flower.

Q: Activity 4. Identify and draw the components of the seeds of pea or gram.

Soak gram seeds overnight and remove the seed coat (testa). The parts identified are: testa with the hilum and micropyle, two large fleshy cotyledons storing food, and the embryo between them consisting of the plumule (future shoot), radicle (future root), epicotyl and hypocotyl. Draw and label all these components.

Q: Activity 5. Perform experiment to investigate the necessary conditions for seed germination.

Place gram seeds in four conditions: (A) dry cotton at room temperature; (B) moist cotton at room temperature with air; (C) moist cotton kept in a refrigerator; (D) seeds fully submerged in boiled, cooled water with an oil layer (no air). Only set B germinates normally, proving that water, suitable temperature and oxygen are all necessary for germination.

Q: Activity 6. Draw different stages of binary fission in amoeba after observing them through slides or charts.

The stages to draw are: the parent Amoeba elongates; its nucleus divides into two; the cytoplasm constricts in the middle; and two daughter amoebae of nearly equal size separate. Label: parent cell, dividing nucleus, constriction and daughter cells.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Home asexual growing: cuttings, tuber pieces, bulbs and Bryophyllum leaf buds.
  • Commercial uses include grafting, cuttings, layering and tissue culture for disease-free plants.
  • Cloning is asexual because the offspring is genetically identical to one parent.
  • Disadvantages of large families outweigh the advantages; STD prevention is a social responsibility.

Q: 1. Grow plants at home using asexual reproduction methods.

At home, grow money plant or mint from stem cuttings placed in water or soil, potato from tuber pieces with eyes, onion and garlic from bulbs, and Bryophyllum from its leaf-margin buds. All these new plants are clones of the parent and grow quickly without seeds.

Q: 2. Describe commercially important applications of asexual reproduction in plants.

Commercially, asexual methods produce uniform crops of identical quality: grafting and budding for mango, citrus and rose varieties; cuttings for sugarcane and grapes; layering for jasmine; and tissue culture for mass production of disease-free banana, potato and orchid plants. They preserve desirable varieties, give earlier yields and multiply seedless fruits.

Q: 3. Justify cloning as a form of asexual reproduction.

In cloning, the nucleus of a body cell of one parent is placed in an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, and the resulting individual is genetically identical to the single parent. Since there is no fertilization and no mixing of genes from two parents, cloning is correctly classed as asexual reproduction.

Q: 4. State the advantages and disadvantages of having large families.

Advantages claimed for large families are more helping hands and earners, support for parents in old age, and companionship among siblings. The disadvantages are greater: income is divided among more members, so food, education and healthcare per child fall; the mother's health suffers; housing becomes crowded; and at national level rapid population growth strains all resources. On balance the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.

Q: 5. Debate the social implications of AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases.

AIDS and other STDs cause long illness and early death, orphan children, and heavy costs on families and the health system. Patients often face stigma and discrimination which discourages testing and treatment. Prevention through awareness, safe medical practices, screened blood and moral conduct is therefore a social responsibility, while patients deserve care and support, not rejection.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Phenotype is the expressed physical trait; genotype is the allele combination.
  • Heterozygous means two different alleles for a single trait.
  • True-breeding green (GG) x yellow (gg) gives all green F1 offspring.
  • AAbb produces only one kind of gamete (Ab).
  • Mendel's main contribution was explaining the patterns of inheritance.

Q: An organism's expressed physical trait, such as seed colour or pod shape, is called its:

(a) Genotype (b) Phenotype (c) Karyotype (d) Physical type
Correct answer: Phenotype

Q: An organism has two different alleles for a single trait. Its genotype is said to be:

(a) Homozygous (b) Heterozygous (c) Hemizygous (d) Homologous
Correct answer: Heterozygous

Q: In the cross-pollination between a true-breeding yellow pod plant and a true-breeding green pod plant, where green pod colour is dominant, the resulting offsprings (F1 generation) will be:

(a) 1/4 green, 3/4 yellow (b) All yellow (c) 1/4 yellow, 3/4 green (d) All green
Correct answer: All green

Q: How many genetically different kinds of gametes an individual with genotype AAbb can produce?

(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 4 (d) 8
Correct answer: 1

Q: Which of the following statements regarding genes is FALSE?

(a) Genes are located on chromosomes (b) Genes consist of a long sequence of DNA (c) A gene contains information for the production of a protein (d) Each cell contains a single copy of every gene
Correct answer: Each cell contains a single copy of every gene

Q: Mendel's primary contribution to our understanding of inheritance was:

(a) The idea that genes are found on chromosomes (b) Explanation of the patterns of inheritance (c) The discovery of alleles (d) Determining that informations contained in DNA are for protein synthesis
Correct answer: Explanation of the patterns of inheritance

Q: A purple-flowered pea plant has the genotype PP. Which of the following statements about this plant is FALSE?

(a) Its phenotype will be white flowers (b) It has a homozygous dominant genotype (c) When bred to a white-flowered plant, all offspring will be purple flowered (d) All the gametes produced will have the same flower colour allele
Correct answer: Its phenotype will be white flowers

Q: Charles Darwin proposed that organisms produce many more offspring than can possible survive on the limited amount of resources available to them. According to Darwin, the offspring that are most likely to survive are those that:

(a) Are born first and grow fastest (b) Are largest and most aggressive (c) Have no natural predators (d) Are best adapted to the environment
Correct answer: Are best adapted to the environment

mcqs.why: Two different alleles for a single trait make the genotype heterozygous, e.g. Tt; identical alleles would be homozygous.

mcqs.why: Working: true-breeding green (GG) x true-breeding yellow (gg) gives all F1 as Gg; green is dominant, so all F1 offspring show green pods.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Genotype is the allele combination (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is its observable expression.
  • Dominant alleles express in homozygous and heterozygous conditions; recessive only in homozygous.
  • Homozygous has identical alleles and is true-breeding; heterozygous has different alleles.
  • Natural selection is by the environment; artificial selection is by humans choosing desired traits.

Q: 1. Define genotype and phenotype.

Genotype is the genetic make-up of an organism, i.e. the combination of alleles it carries for a trait, e.g. TT, Tt or tt. Phenotype is the observable expression of the genotype, i.e. the actual trait shown by the organism, e.g. tall or dwarf plant.

Q: 2. What do you mean by dominant and recessive alleles?

A dominant allele is the allele which expresses itself in both homozygous and heterozygous condition and masks the other allele, e.g. the allele for tallness (T) in pea. A recessive allele expresses itself only in the homozygous condition and remains hidden in the presence of the dominant allele, e.g. the allele for dwarfness (t).

Q: 3. What are the homozygous and heterozygous genotypes?

A homozygous genotype has two identical alleles for a trait, e.g. TT (homozygous dominant) or tt (homozygous recessive); such an organism is true-breeding. A heterozygous genotype has two different alleles for a trait, e.g. Tt; only the dominant trait appears in its phenotype, but it carries the recessive allele.

Q: 4. Differentiate between natural and artificial selection.

In natural selection the environment selects the organisms best adapted to survive and reproduce, without human involvement, and it leads to evolution over long periods. In artificial selection humans deliberately choose organisms with desired traits and breed them, producing improved varieties of plants and animals in a few generations.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Chromatin is DNA wound around histone proteins forming nucleosomes.
  • Law of segregation: alleles separate in gamete formation; F2 phenotypic ratio 3:1.
  • Dihybrid F2 ratio 9:3:3:1 proves the law of independent assortment.
  • Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate heterozygote (pink Mirabilis), F2 1:2:1.
  • Co-dominance expresses both alleles fully, e.g. blood group AB (IA IB).

Q: 1. Describe the structure of chromatin.

Chromatin is the material of chromosomes, made of DNA and proteins (mainly histones). DNA winds around histone proteins forming bead-like units called nucleosomes, and the string of nucleosomes coils and folds into thicker fibres. During cell division the chromatin condenses further to form the visible chromosomes. Chromatin carries the genes in its DNA.

Q: 2. Describe Mendel's law of segregation.

The law of segregation states that the two alleles of a gene present in an individual separate (segregate) from each other during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one allele. As a result, a heterozygous (Tt) parent produces two kinds of gametes, T and t, in equal numbers, and the recessive trait reappears in the F2 generation in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

Q: 3. Explain how Mendel proved the law of independent assortment.

Mendel crossed pea plants differing in two traits (dihybrid cross): yellow round seeds (YYRR) with green wrinkled seeds (yyrr). The F1 were all yellow round. In F2 he obtained 9 yellow round, 3 yellow wrinkled, 3 green round and 1 green wrinkled (9:3:3:1), including new combinations not present in the parents. This proved that the alleles of different genes assort into gametes independently of one another — the law of independent assortment.

Q: 4. How would you prove that variations lead to evolution?

Variations produced by mutations, crossing over and random fusion of gametes make individuals of a population different. Those with variations favourable for the environment survive and reproduce more (natural selection), passing the variations to offspring. Over many generations such selected variations accumulate and the population changes into a new form, i.e. evolution occurs. Examples include the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and the varieties of wild mustard produced by selection of variations.

Q: 5. Explain the phenomenon of incomplete dominance with the help of example.

In incomplete dominance neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygous phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygous phenotypes. Example: in the four-o'clock plant (Mirabilis), crossing a red-flowered plant (RR) with a white-flowered plant (rr) gives all pink-flowered plants (Rr) in F1. Self-pollination of F1 gives red, pink and white in a 1:2:1 ratio in F2.

Q: 6. What do you mean by co-dominance. Give an example.

In co-dominance both alleles of a heterozygous genotype express themselves fully and side by side in the phenotype, and neither is dominant or recessive. Example: in the ABO blood group system, a person with genotype IA IB has blood group AB, in which both A and B antigens are produced equally on the red blood cells.

lessons.title: The Terms to Know
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Allele is an alternative form of a gene at the same locus.
  • Gene is a unit of inheritance; a DNA sequence coding for a protein.
  • Locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome.
  • Mutation is a sudden change in DNA or a gene producing a new trait.

Q: Define: Allele

An alternative form of a gene present at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

Q: Define: Artificial selection

The selection and breeding of organisms with desired traits by humans.

Q: Define: Breeds

Distinct varieties of a domesticated animal produced by artificial selection.

Q: Define: Chromatin

The DNA-and-protein material of the nucleus which condenses to form chromosomes.

Q: Define: Co-dominance

The condition in which both alleles of a heterozygote are fully expressed.

Q: Define: Cultivar

A cultivated variety of a plant produced by artificial selection.

Q: Define: Dihybrid cross

A cross between organisms differing in two traits controlled by two genes.

Q: Define: Dominant

The allele (or trait) which is expressed in both homozygous and heterozygous conditions.

Q: Define: Gene

A unit of inheritance; a specific sequence of DNA coding for a protein.

Q: Define: Genotype

The genetic make-up of an organism for a trait.

Q: Define: Heterozygous

Having two different alleles for a gene, e.g. Tt.

Q: Define: Histone

The protein around which DNA is wound in chromatin.

Q: Define: Homologous chromosomes

A pair of chromosomes of the same length and shape carrying genes for the same traits.

Q: Define: Homozygous

Having two identical alleles for a gene, e.g. TT or tt.

Q: Define: Incomplete dominance

The condition in which the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype.

Q: Define: Inheritance

The transmission of traits from parents to offspring through genes.

Q: Define: Locus

The fixed position of a gene on a chromosome.

Q: Define: Monohybrid cross

A cross between organisms differing in one trait controlled by one gene.

Q: Define: Mutation

A sudden change in the DNA or gene which produces a new trait.

Q: Define: Natural selection

The selection of best-adapted organisms by the environment, leading to evolution.

Q: Define: Nucleosome

A unit of chromatin in which DNA is wound around a group of histone proteins.

Q: Define: Organic evolution

The gradual change of organisms over generations producing new species.

Q: Define: Phenotype

The observable expression of a genotype.

Q: Define: Recessive trait

The trait which appears only in the homozygous condition.

Q: Define: Trait

An inherited characteristic of an organism, e.g. seed colour.

Q: Define: True-breeding

Producing offspring identical to the parents for a trait (homozygous).

Q: Define: Variations

Differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
