lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Controlling genes could cure genetic diseases but raises ethical questions.
  • Advances include gene therapy, CRISPR, DNA testing and Bt cotton.
  • A gene is transcribed to mRNA then translated at ribosomes into protein.
  • Punnett squares predict offspring genotypes, phenotypes and ratios, e.g. Tt x Tt gives 3:1.

Q: 1. Describe various possibilities if humans could be able to control the functioning of genes.

If gene functioning could be controlled, defective genes could be switched off or corrected to cure genetic diseases, insulin and other proteins could be produced on demand, crops and animals could be given desired traits, and ageing processes might be slowed. It would also raise ethical questions about selecting traits in unborn children, so careful regulation would be needed.

Q: 2. Prepare a report using newspaper clippings on the recent advances and future possibilities in genetics.

Model report points: recent advances include gene therapy trials for inherited blindness and blood disorders, CRISPR gene editing, DNA testing for disease risk and forensic identification, and genetically modified crops in Pakistan such as Bt cotton. Future possibilities include personalized medicines matched to a patient's genes, cures for more genetic diseases, and crops resistant to drought and pests. (Compile the report from current newspaper clippings under these headings.)

Q: 3. Rationalize life as a product of the diversity brought about by chromosomes, genes and DNA.

DNA carries genes arranged on chromosomes, and changes in them (mutations, recombination and independent assortment) create the enormous diversity of traits among organisms. Natural selection preserves useful combinations, so over time this genetic diversity has produced the variety of life forms on Earth, each adapted to its environment.

Q: 4. Outline the scientific findings and some of the technological advances that led to the modern concept of gene.

Mendel's experiments showed that traits are controlled by discrete factors; Sutton and Boveri linked these factors to chromosomes; Morgan proved genes lie on chromosomes; Avery and then Watson and Crick showed that genes are made of DNA and revealed its double-helix structure. Microscopes, X-ray crystallography, DNA sequencing and recombinant DNA technology then refined the gene concept to a specific DNA sequence coding for a protein.

Q: 5. Analyse the concept of gene to produce various proteins of the body.

Each gene is a DNA sequence carrying the coded instructions for one polypeptide. During protein synthesis the gene is transcribed into mRNA, which is translated at ribosomes into an amino-acid chain that folds into a protein. Different genes thus produce the enzymes, hormones, antibodies and structural proteins of the body, and switching genes on or off in different cells produces the needed proteins in each tissue.

Q: 6. Describe the importance of scientific investigation and mathematical know how in genetics.

Genetics depends on careful experiments with counted offspring and on probability and ratios (such as 3:1 and 9:3:3:1) to test whether results match predictions. Punnett squares, percentages and statistical tests let scientists infer genotypes, predict crosses and confirm laws of inheritance; without mathematics Mendel's own results could not have been interpreted.

Q: 7. Explain how genetics can predict the progeny of two individuals which are crossed.

Knowing the genotypes of the parents and the dominance of alleles, the possible gametes of each parent are listed and combined in a Punnett square. The squares give the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring and their ratios, e.g. a cross Tt x Tt predicts about 3 tall to 1 dwarf offspring. Such predictions are used in plant and animal breeding and in genetic counselling.

Q: 8. What is the role of environment on the selection of better variations?

The environment decides which variations are 'better': a variation useful in one environment (e.g. thick fur in cold regions, drought resistance in dry regions) may be useless in another. Environmental factors such as climate, food, predators and diseases therefore act as the selecting agents of natural selection, and also modify the expression of genes, as nutrition affects height.

lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Ecological organization runs from individual organism to population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
  • An ecosystem has biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components (light, water, air, soil).
  • Energy flows one way and is lost as heat, while materials are recycled in biogeochemical cycles.
  • The 3Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle for conserving natural resources.

Q: 1. What are the different levels of ecological organization?

From smallest to largest: individual organism, population (individuals of one species in an area), community (populations of different species living together), ecosystem (community plus its abiotic environment), biome (a large region of a particular climate and life), and the biosphere (all ecosystems of the Earth together).

Q: 2. Define ecosystem and its components.

An ecosystem is a self-sustaining unit consisting of a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their physical environment. Its components are biotic (producers, consumers and decomposers) and abiotic (light, temperature, water, air, soil and minerals).

Q: 3. How the flow of energy is different from that of materials?

Energy flows through the ecosystem in one direction only: it enters as sunlight, passes from producers to consumers and decomposers, and is lost as heat at every trophic level, so it must be supplied continuously. Materials such as carbon, nitrogen, water and minerals are not lost; they are recycled again and again between organisms and the environment in biogeochemical cycles.

Q: 4. Define food chain and food web.

A food chain is a simple linear sequence showing who eats whom in an ecosystem, e.g. grass, then rabbit, then fox. A food web is the interconnected network of many food chains in an ecosystem, showing that most organisms eat and are eaten by several species.

Q: 5. What do you mean by the concept of 3Rs with reference to the conservation of natural resources?

The 3Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. Reduce means using less of resources such as water, energy and materials; Reuse means using items again instead of throwing them away; Recycle means processing waste materials (paper, plastic, metal, glass) into new products. Following the 3Rs conserves natural resources and reduces pollution.

mcqs.why: The levels run from the individual organism, through population and community, up to ecosystem, biome and biosphere.

All ecosystems of the Earth together
mcqs.why: A community is made up of populations of different species that live together and interact in an area.

A community plus its abiotic environment
Individuals of one species in an area
All ecosystems of the Earth together
mcqs.why: The biosphere is the largest level, comprising all the ecosystems of the Earth taken together as a whole.

mcqs.why: Producers are living organisms, while light, temperature and soil are abiotic, non-living components of ecosystems.

mcqs.why: Water is a non-living abiotic factor, whereas producers, consumers and decomposers are the biotic components.

options: Using items again instead of throwing them away

mcqs.why: Reduce means using less of resources such as water, energy and materials so that fewer resources are consumed.

options: They flow one way and are lost as heat

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pyramids of numbers and biomass show numbers and total dry mass at each trophic level, decreasing upwards.
  • The carbon cycle moves carbon between air, organisms, fossil fuels, limestone and oceans.
  • The nitrogen cycle has fixation, absorption, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification stages.
  • Competition, predation and symbiosis (mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) are major species interactions.

Q: 1. Explain what do you mean by the pyramids of number and biomass.

A pyramid of numbers shows the number of organisms at each trophic level of a food chain; producers are the most numerous and top consumers the fewest (though a single large tree supporting many insects gives an inverted base exception). A pyramid of biomass shows the total dry mass of organisms at each trophic level; biomass decreases at each higher level because most energy and material is lost in respiration, excretion and uneaten parts.

Q: 2. Write a note on Carbon cycle.

Carbon dioxide of the air is fixed by plants in photosynthesis and becomes part of plant and then animal bodies through feeding. Carbon returns to the air by the respiration of all organisms, by decomposition of dead bodies and wastes, and by burning of fossil fuels and wood. Some carbon is stored for long periods in fossil fuels, limestone and ocean water. The cycle keeps the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere nearly constant, though human burning of fuels is now increasing it.

Q: 3. What are the different stages of Nitrogen cycle?

(1) Nitrogen fixation: atmospheric nitrogen is converted to ammonia/nitrates by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in soil and root nodules) and by lightning. (2) Absorption: plants absorb nitrates and make proteins; animals get nitrogen by eating plants. (3) Ammonification: decomposers convert proteins and wastes of dead organisms into ammonia. (4) Nitrification: bacteria convert ammonia to nitrites and then nitrates. (5) Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas, completing the cycle.

Q: 4. Write notes on competition, predation and symbiosis.

Competition is the struggle between organisms for the same limited resources such as food, space and light; it may be intraspecific (within a species) or interspecific (between species). Predation is the interaction in which one organism (predator) hunts, kills and eats another (prey), e.g. lion and deer. Symbiosis is the close living together of two species, including mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected) and parasitism (one benefits and harms the other).

Q: 5. Explain how human activities have contributed to the loss of balance in nature.

Humans have disturbed natural balance by deforestation, over-hunting and over-grazing, excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides, industrial and vehicle pollution, and rapid population growth. These activities destroy habitats, reduce biodiversity, upset food webs and cycles, and cause global warming and eutrophication, so ecosystems can no longer regulate themselves as before.

Q: 6. Write note on the causes and effects of the air and water pollutions.

Air pollution is caused by smoke and gases from vehicles, factories, burning of fuels and waste; it causes respiratory diseases, acid rain, smog and global warming. Water pollution is caused by sewage, industrial effluents, fertilizers and pesticides entering water bodies; it kills aquatic life, causes eutrophication and spreads diseases such as cholera, typhoid and hepatitis in people who use the polluted water.

mcqs.q: What does a pyramid of numbers show?
options: Number of organisms at each trophic level
Total dry mass at each trophic level
Total energy stored in producers only
Movement of carbon through the air
mcqs.why: A pyramid of numbers shows the number of organisms present at each trophic level of a food chain.

mcqs.q: Why does biomass decrease at each higher trophic level?
options: Because most energy and material is lost in respiration, excretion and uneaten parts
Because top consumers reproduce very fast
mcqs.why: Biomass decreases because most energy and material is lost through respiration, excretion and uneaten parts.

mcqs.q: How is carbon dioxide of the air first fixed in the carbon cycle?
mcqs.why: Plants fix atmospheric carbon dioxide in photosynthesis, and it then passes to animals through feeding.

mcqs.q: Which process returns carbon to the air in the carbon cycle?
mcqs.why: Carbon returns to the air by respiration of all organisms, as well as by decomposition and burning of fuels.

mcqs.q: What happens during ammonification in the nitrogen cycle?
options: Nitrates are converted back to nitrogen gas
Ammonia is converted to nitrites and nitrates
Decomposers convert proteins and wastes of dead organisms into ammonia
mcqs.why: During ammonification, decomposers convert proteins and wastes of dead organisms into ammonia in the soil.

mcqs.q: What happens during nitrification?
options: Bacteria convert ammonia to nitrites and then nitrates
Bacteria convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas
Plants absorb nitrates to make proteins
mcqs.why: In nitrification, bacteria convert ammonia first to nitrites and then to nitrates, which plants can absorb.

mcqs.q: What is denitrification?
options: Conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia by bacteria
Conversion of nitrates back to nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria
Conversion of ammonia into nitrates by bacteria
Absorption of nitrates by plant roots

lessons.title: The Terms to Know
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Abiotic factors are non-living, while decomposers recycle dead bodies and wastes.
  • Ammonification, nitrification and denitrification are key nitrogen-cycle processes.
  • Commensalism, mutualism and parasitism describe different symbiotic interactions.
  • Eutrophication is algal overgrowth from extra nutrients that depletes oxygen in water.

Q: Define: Abiotic

The non-living components of an ecosystem, e.g. light, water, air and soil.

Q: Define: Acid Rain

Rain made acidic by dissolved sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from polluted air.

Q: Define: Ammonification

The conversion of proteins and wastes of dead organisms into ammonia by decomposers.

Q: Define: Atmospheric nitrogen fixation

The conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into compounds by lightning and rain.

Q: Define: Biogeochemical Cycle

The cyclic movement of materials (carbon, nitrogen, water) between organisms and the environment.

Q: Define: Biological nitrogen fixation

The conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia by nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

Q: Define: Biosphere

The part of the Earth where life exists; the sum of all ecosystems.

Q: Define: Biotic

The living components of an ecosystem.

Q: Define: Carbon cycle

The cyclic movement of carbon between the atmosphere, organisms, oceans and rocks.

Q: Define: Carnivore

An animal which eats other animals.

Q: Define: Commensalism

An interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

Q: Define: Competition

The struggle among organisms for the same limited resources.

Q: Define: Consumer

An organism which feeds on other organisms for food.

Q: Define: Decomposer

An organism (bacteria, fungi) which breaks down dead bodies and wastes, recycling materials.

Q: Define: Deforestation

The cutting and removal of forests over large areas.

Q: Define: Denitrification

The conversion of nitrates back into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria.

Q: Define: Ecological pyramid

A diagram showing numbers, biomass or energy at successive trophic levels.

Q: Define: Environment

The surroundings of an organism, including living and non-living factors affecting it.

Q: Define: Eutrophication

The excessive growth of algae in water due to extra nutrients, which depletes oxygen and kills aquatic life.

Q: Define: Food chain

A linear sequence of organisms showing who eats whom.

Q: Define: Food web

The interconnected network of food chains in an ecosystem.

Q: Define: Global Warming

The gradual rise in Earth's temperature due to increased greenhouse gases.

Q: Define: Interspecific interactions

Interactions between individuals of different species.

Q: Define: Intraspecific interactions

Interactions between individuals of the same species.

Q: Define: Mutualism

An interaction in which both species benefit.

Q: Define: Natural resources

Materials supplied by nature useful to humans, e.g. water, forests, minerals.

Q: Define: Nitrification

The conversion of ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates by bacteria.

Q: Define: Nitrogen cycle

The cyclic movement of nitrogen between the air, soil and organisms.

Q: Define: Nitrogen fixation

The conversion of nitrogen gas into usable compounds (ammonia or nitrates).

Q: Define: Non-renewable resources

Resources which are used up and not replaced naturally in a short time, e.g. fossil fuels.

Q: Define: Overpopulation

Population larger than the resources of an area can support.

Q: Define: Ozone

A form of oxygen in the upper atmosphere which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays.

Q: Define: Parasitism

An interaction in which one organism (parasite) benefits and the other (host) is harmed.

Q: Define: Phytoplankton

Microscopic floating plants which are the main producers of aquatic ecosystems.

Q: Define: Pollutant

A harmful substance added to the environment.

Q: Define: Pollution

The addition of harmful substances to the environment, damaging life.

Q: Define: Predation

The interaction in which a predator kills and eats its prey.

Q: Define: Producer

An organism (green plant) which makes its own food by photosynthesis.

Q: Define: Pyramid of biomass

A pyramid showing the total dry mass of organisms at each trophic level.

Q: Define: Pyramid of numbers

A pyramid showing the number of organisms at each trophic level.

Q: Define: Renewable resources

Resources which are naturally replaced, e.g. air, water, forests.

Q: Define: Symbiosis

The close living association between two different species.

Key Points

  • A pond's biotic factors include phytoplankton, plants, insects, frogs, fish and decomposers.

Q: Activity 1. Make a visit to a pond and compare the abiotic and biotic factors of a pond with that of an aquarium.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A city or village is an ecosystem where humans act as consumers with a duty to conserve resources.
  • Overpopulation increases competition for food, water, jobs and services, causing poverty and unemployment.
  • Pakistan's population grew from about 108 million in 1990 to about 190 million in 2015.
  • Community problems like garbage and smoke are solved by waste management, plantation and awareness.

Q: 1. State how your city or village is an ecosystem and describe your position and role in that ecosystem.

A city or village contains living organisms (people, animals, plants, microbes) interacting with abiotic factors (air, water, soil, buildings and climate), with flows of energy and materials, so it is an ecosystem. My position is that of a consumer; my role includes using resources, producing waste, and — responsibly — conserving water and energy, planting trees and keeping the environment clean so the ecosystem stays balanced.

Q: 2. Describe the possible consequences of competition (due to limited resources and overpopulation) in human society.

When population grows beyond available resources, competition increases for food, water, land, jobs, education and health facilities. The consequences are poverty, unemployment, rising prices, overcrowding, conflicts and crime, and greater pressure on the environment. Planning population and fair distribution of resources reduce these consequences.

Q: 3. Use data from internet and literature search on Pakistan population growth from 1990 to 2015 and interpret this population growth and the possible consequences on our society.

Pakistan's population grew from about 108 million in 1990 to about 190 million in 2015, one of the highest growth rates in the region. Interpretation: such rapid growth doubles the demand for food, water, housing, schools and hospitals in one generation, increases unemployment and poverty, over-exploits groundwater and forests, and slows development unless population growth is controlled and resources are planned.

Q: 4. Identify environmental problems in your community. What are the causes and what should be done to solve these problems?

Common problems: garbage dumped in streets and drains, smoke from vehicles and brick kilns, polluted drinking water, and cutting of trees. Causes are careless disposal, lack of services and low awareness. Solutions: proper waste collection and disposal, sewage treatment, tree plantation, vehicle emission checks, and community awareness campaigns with enforcement of environmental laws.

Q: 5. Actively participate in the community efforts for the conservation of nature.

Participation includes joining tree-plantation and cleanliness drives, protecting local birds and trees, saving water and electricity, separating and recycling household waste, and motivating neighbours to do the same. A written record of one such activity, with its results, should be presented in class.

Q: 6. Organize a poster or picture exhibition at school on some environmental topic.

Plan: choose a topic such as 'Save Water' or 'Stop Air Pollution'; prepare posters showing the problem, its causes and its solutions with pictures and short captions; display them in a school corridor or hall; and invite classes to view and discuss them. The exhibition spreads awareness and encourages students to act for conservation.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Fermentation breaks down carbohydrates by microorganisms, usually without oxygen, in fermenters.
  • Ethanol is made by Saccharomyces and lactic products by lactic acid bacteria from milk.

Q: 1. How would you define fermentation with reference to biotechnology?

In biotechnology, fermentation is the process in which microorganisms such as yeast and bacteria break down carbohydrates, usually in the absence of oxygen, in controlled vessels (fermenters) to produce useful products such as ethanol, lactic acid, antibiotics and enzymes on a commercial scale.

Q: 2. Name any two industrial products made by fermentation. Also describe their uses in the industry.

(1) Ethanol, produced by yeast (Saccharomyces) from sugar solutions; it is used as a fuel (gasohol), as a solvent, and in medicines and beverages. (2) Lactic acid / yogurt and cheese, produced by lactic acid bacteria from milk; these are food products, and lactic acid is also used in the food and pharmaceutical industries. Penicillin and citric acid are other important fermentation products.

Q: 3. What are the products of the two types of carbohydrate fermentation?

In alcoholic fermentation, glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide (by yeast). In lactic acid fermentation, glucose is converted into lactic acid (by lactic acid bacteria, and temporarily in muscles). Both types release a small amount of energy and take place without oxygen.

Q: 4. Give an example how biotechnology is helping for better environment.

Biotechnology produces microorganisms which degrade pollutants: bacteria are used to clean oil spills, to treat sewage and industrial waste water, and to remove sulfur from coal. Biofertilizers and biopesticides also reduce the use of harmful chemical fertilizers and pesticides, keeping the environment cleaner.

Q: 5. In biotechnology, what is meant by Genetically Modified Organism (GMO)? How is it made?

A GMO is an organism whose genes have been deliberately changed by genetic engineering, usually by inserting a gene from another organism. It is made by isolating the gene of interest, inserting it into a vector (such as a plasmid) to form recombinant DNA, transferring this DNA into the host organism, and then selecting and growing the organisms which express the new gene, e.g. Bt cotton.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms or their parts to produce medicines, foods and useful processes.
  • A fermenter grows microorganisms under controlled conditions; fermentation may be batch or continuous.
  • Genetic engineering steps are isolation, insertion into a vector, transfer, selection and growth.
  • Single-cell proteins from microorganisms are a rich, quickly produced protein supplement.

Q: 1. Define biotechnology and describe its importance.

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells or their parts to make useful products and processes for human welfare. It is important because it produces medicines such as insulin, vaccines and antibiotics, improves crops for yield and resistance, provides foods like cheese and yogurt, helps clean the environment, and supplies single-cell protein and biofuels.

Q: 2. What is a fermenter? What are the two types of fermentation carried out in fermenters?

A fermenter is a large closed vessel in which microorganisms are grown under controlled conditions of temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients for the industrial production of useful substances. The two types of fermentation are: batch fermentation, in which nutrients are added once and the product is collected at the end; and continuous fermentation, in which nutrients are added continuously and the product is removed continuously.

Q: 3. Describe the achievements of genetic engineering in medicine, agriculture and environment.

Medicine: production of human insulin, growth hormone, interferons and vaccines by engineered bacteria, and gene therapy for genetic diseases. Agriculture: insect-resistant Bt cotton, virus-resistant and high-yielding crop varieties, and animals producing more milk and meat. Environment: engineered bacteria that degrade oil spills and pollutants, biofertilizers and biopesticides that reduce chemical pollution.

Q: 4. What basic steps a genetic engineer adopts during the manipulation of genes?

The basic steps are: (1) isolation of the gene of interest from the donor DNA, cutting it with restriction endonuclease enzymes; (2) insertion of the gene into a vector (plasmid) to make recombinant DNA; (3) transfer of the recombinant DNA into the host organism; (4) selection of the transformed host cells; and (5) growth of the modified organism and extraction of the desired product.

Q: 5. What are single cell proteins? Describe their importance.

Single-cell proteins (SCP) are the proteins obtained from the cells of microorganisms such as algae, fungi (yeast), bacteria and Spirulina, grown on cheap raw materials and wastes. They are important as a rich protein supplement for human food and animal feed, they can be produced quickly in small space throughout the year, and their production also helps use up industrial and agricultural wastes.

Q: Activity 1. Investigate the role of yeast in the fermentation of flour.

Mix flour, warm water, sugar and yeast into a dough and keep it in a warm place beside an identical dough without yeast. This shows yeast's role in making bread light and spongy.

Q: Activity 2. Investigate the role of bacteria in the fermentation of milk.

Add a spoonful of yogurt (containing Lactobacillus bacteria) to warm milk and keep it undisturbed for several hours; a control sample of milk receives no yogurt. The inoculated milk sets into yogurt and tastes sour because the bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid, which coagulates the milk protein. The control remains liquid milk.

lessons.notes_html:

Q: 1. Apply knowledge to identify different products of animal and human food having single-cell proteins.

Single-cell protein products include Spirulina tablets and powders used as a protein-rich health food, yeast extracts and protein supplements, Quorn-type mycoprotein foods made from fungi, and SCP-enriched animal and poultry feeds produced from bacteria and yeast grown on industrial wastes.

Q: 2. Develop awareness among the students of other classes about important social and ethical issues of genetic engineering.

Awareness points for a class talk or poster: benefits of genetic engineering must be balanced against concerns such as the safety of GM foods, possible effects of released GMOs on wild species, patenting of life forms, and the ethics of human gene editing and cloning. Q: 3. Describe the ways in which our society can benefit from the knowledge of genetic engineering.

Society benefits through cheaper and purer medicines (insulin, vaccines), treatment of genetic diseases, higher and more resistant crop yields improving food security, better livestock, forensic DNA identification, and cleaner industry and environment through engineered microorganisms.

Q: 4. Interpret the data collected from internet on virus resistant, insect resistant and high yielding varieties of agricultural crops in Pakistan.

Key Points

Q: 1. Define pharmacology and distinguish it from pharmacy.

Pharmacology is the branch of science which studies the action of drugs on the body: their sources, effects, mechanisms and uses. Pharmacy is the profession and practice of preparing, compounding and dispensing medicines to patients. Pharmacology is thus the scientific study of drugs, while pharmacy is the practical art of making medicines available.

Q: 2. Differentiate between medicinal drug and addictive drug.

A medicinal drug is a substance used for the treatment, cure, prevention or diagnosis of disease, taken in prescribed doses. An addictive drug is a substance which produces physical and psychological dependence; the user craves it repeatedly and suffers withdrawal symptoms on stopping, e.g. heroin and morphine. Some drugs, like morphine, are medicinal when used under prescription but addictive when misused.

Q: 3. Differentiate between analgesic and antibiotic.

An analgesic is a drug which relieves pain without causing loss of consciousness, e.g. aspirin and paracetamol. An antibiotic is a drug obtained from microorganisms (or made synthetically) which kills or stops the growth of bacteria and is used to treat bacterial infections, e.g. penicillin.

Q: 4. What is marijuana? To which category of addictive drugs, it belongs?

Marijuana is a drug obtained from the plant Cannabis sativa (hemp), containing the active substance THC. It belongs to the category of hallucinogens, the addictive drugs which alter perception, mood and thought.

Q: 5. Differentiate between narcotics and hallucinogens.

Narcotics are addictive drugs which depress the central nervous system, relieve severe pain and produce sleep and a feeling of well-being, e.g. morphine and heroin; they cause strong physical dependence. Hallucinogens are addictive drugs which alter perception and thinking and produce hallucinations (seeing or hearing unreal things), e.g. marijuana and LSD; their dependence is mainly psychological.

lessons.title: Understanding the Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Drugs come from plants, animals, microorganisms, minerals and synthetic sources.
  • Sedatives calm the nervous system, narcotics are strong addictive pain-relievers, hallucinogens distort perception.
  • Antibiotic groups include penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines and sulfonamides with different actions.
  • Incomplete antibiotic courses cause resistance; vaccines work through antibodies and memory cells.

Q: 1. What are the sources of drugs? Give examples.

Drugs are obtained from: (1) Plants, e.g. opium and morphine from poppy, quinine from cinchona bark, digitalis from foxglove. (2) Animals, e.g. insulin from pancreas, antivenoms and hormones. (3) Microorganisms, e.g. penicillin from the fungus Penicillium and other antibiotics. (4) Minerals, e.g. iron salts, iodine and Epsom salt. (5) Synthetic (laboratory-made) sources, e.g. aspirin, paracetamol and sulfonamides.

Q: 2. Write a note on sedatives, narcotics and hallucinogens.

Sedatives are drugs which calm the nervous system and reduce anxiety and excitement, inducing sleep in larger doses, e.g. diazepam; their misuse causes dependence. Narcotics are strong pain-relieving drugs which depress the central nervous system and cause deep sleep and addiction, e.g. morphine, codeine and heroin. Hallucinogens distort perception, mood and thought and produce hallucinations, e.g. marijuana and LSD; they damage mental health and behaviour. All three groups are addictive and harmful when used without medical supervision.

Q: 3. Describe the main groups of antibiotics.

The main groups are: (1) Penicillins, e.g. penicillin and amoxicillin, which stop the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall. (2) Cephalosporins, similar to penicillins in action, e.g. cephalosporin. (3) Tetracyclines, broad-spectrum antibiotics which inhibit protein synthesis in bacteria. (4) Sulfonamides (sulfa drugs), synthetic antibiotics which stop the synthesis of folic acid in bacteria. Antibiotics may be bactericidal (killing bacteria) or bacteriostatic (stopping their growth).

Q: 4. Write a note on resistance against antibiotics.

When antibiotics are used unnecessarily, in wrong doses, or the course is left incomplete, the sensitive bacteria are killed but resistant bacteria survive and multiply, producing a population on which the antibiotic no longer works. This antibiotic resistance is a growing danger, making infections harder to treat. It can be reduced by using antibiotics only on a doctor's prescription, in the correct dose and for the full prescribed course.

Q: 5. Describe the mode of action of vaccines.

A vaccine contains weakened or killed pathogens, or their parts (antigens). When introduced into the body, it stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells against that pathogen, without causing the disease. If the real pathogen later attacks, the memory cells respond rapidly and strongly, destroying it before illness develops. Vaccines thus give long-lasting protection (immunity) against viral and bacterial diseases.

lessons.title: Science, Technology and Society
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Common painkillers in Pakistan include paracetamol and aspirin; antibiotics include amoxicillin and penicillin; diazepam is a sedative.
  • Narcotics and hallucinogens cause family breakdown, crime, disease spread through shared needles and accidents.
  • Over-dosage of antibiotics damages liver and kidneys; under-dosage creates resistant strains.
  • Antibiotics must be used only in the dose and duration prescribed by a doctor.

Q: 1. Compile a list of various painkillers, antibiotics and sedatives being used in our Pakistan.

Painkillers (analgesics) commonly used: paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen and diclofenac. Antibiotics: amoxicillin, penicillin, cephalosporins, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline and sulfonamides. Sedatives: diazepam and similar prescription medicines. All of these, especially antibiotics and sedatives, should be used only on a doctor's advice.

Q: 2. Summarize the antisocial effects of the usage of hallucinogens and narcotics.

Drug users neglect family and work, lose income and often turn to theft and crime to buy drugs; families break up and children suffer. Addicts spread diseases through shared needles, cause road accidents, and burden hospitals and society. Drug trafficking also fuels organized crime and corruption, so these drugs damage the whole social fabric.

Q: 3. Justify the effects of possible over-dosage, under-dosage and drug interactions when using antibiotics without doctor's consultation.

Over-dosage of antibiotics can poison the body and damage the liver, kidneys and useful gut bacteria. Under-dosage or an incomplete course fails to kill all bacteria and creates resistant strains, so the infection returns in a stronger form. Antibiotics taken with other medicines can interact, reducing each other's effect or causing harmful side effects. Therefore antibiotics must be used only in the dose and duration prescribed by a doctor.
